state.case_summary:
A 50-year-old woman with hypertension and COPD first presented 5 months before admission with lower abdominal pain and decreased bowel movements; she was diagnosed with constipation. One month later, she returned with left lower-quadrant pain and low-grade fevers and was treated with ciprofloxacin and metronidazole for presumed diverticulitis. Symptoms partially improved, but she then had right upper-quadrant pain; abdominal CT was performed and incidentally revealed a confluent retroperitoneal soft-tissue mass encasing surrounding vessels. A HIDA scan confirmed cholecystitis, and she underwent cholecystectomy. 

One month after surgery, she had 5 days of progressively worsening, constant epigastric pain with nausea, vomiting, fatigue, anorexia, decreased urine output, and a 20-lb weight loss over 4 months. She denied fevers, chills, dysuria, or GI bleeding. On exam, blood pressure was 162/91 mmHg, pulse 79, and she had slight epigastric tenderness without guarding. Labs showed sodium 146 mEq/L, potassium 5.1 mEq/L, creatinine 8.18 mg/dL (baseline 0.8), WBC 10.4 K/uL, hemoglobin 13.1 g/dL, and platelets 383 K/uL. Renal ultrasound demonstrated mild bilateral hydronephrosis, and postrenal obstruction was suspected. 

The following morning, a retrograde pyelogram showed bilateral hydronephrosis with extrinsic compression and medial deviation of the ureters, most prominently on the right. Ureteral stents were placed, relieving her obstruction, and her renal function subsequently returned to baseline.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis
B. after AKI and hydronephrosis on ultrasound
C. Diverticulitis was initially considered due to left lower
D. Cholecystitis was diagnosed when right upper
E. Postrenal uropathy was suspected after AKI and hydronephrosis on ultrasound
F. Malignancy was excluded by biopsy showing only inflammation
G. Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis was diagnosed based on the imaging triad of hydroureteronephrosis, medial
H. None

root.label: Chronic-Progressive Abdominal Pain Syndrome with Renal Failure and Bilateral Hydronephrosis
excluded_candidates: Mechanical bowel obstruction: ruled out by cholecystectomy and lack of GI bleeding
Inflammatory bowel disease: less likely given the absence of GI bleeding and lack of response to ciprofloxacin and metronidazole
Metastatic cancer: possible but not directly supported by the evidence
